Development guide

Tech Radar

Fifty-one products and tools, grouped by the job they do in an agent stack. Each group explains what that type of product is for, then lists the options with what each one does, how it is supplied, and its current status.

A note on Tech Radar

This page is still a draft and may not reflect the latest technologies or releases.

The entries are based on published documentation, not local deployment tests. Carry out your own research before adopting any option.

Key points

  • Start with the job you need done, then compare the options inside that group.
  • Scope is AWS; managed Claude or OpenAI through Bedrock is the default route, with direct APIs as exceptions.
  • Versions are dated 17 November 2026. Command-line tools and SDKs ship weekly, so confirm the current version before adoption.

How to read this radar

Each group below opens with a short description of what that type of product is and when to use it, then a table of the products in the group. The table says what each product does, how it is supplied, and its status. A status of Do not use means do not adopt it from this reference; the linked Tech Scan page gives the safer route or the retirement date.

Labels on this page

Available
Generally available or actively maintained, and usable from this reference.
Emerging
In preview, early access, or new and still settling. Prove it on representative work before adoption.
Hold
Usable only with conditions, such as a pinned version, a licence check, or a named limitation. Read the entry before adopting it.
Do not use
Do not adopt from this reference: retired, winding down, dormant, or not recommended for approval.

The first version of this page showed a popularity signal and a sentiment signal for each product. Those two columns are gone: they mixed download counts, opinion and licence into one phrase, so they did not help a reader compare options. The replacement columns say what the product does, how it is supplied, and its status. Versions are dated 17 November 2026, and a version that moves weekly will be out of date soon after that; the Sources list gives the vendor page or repository where the current version can be confirmed.

Check before adoption

  • Exact product, version, endpoint, model or inference profile, and region
  • Licence and hosting, including where data travels and whether the region you need is supported
  • Fast-moving command-line tools and SDKs pinned to an exact version, not tracking latest
  • Retired and winding-down products excluded, with the replacement named in the linked reference
  • Route proved on representative work, with failures retained, before wider adoption

Models and model access

These products choose the model and reach it. The AWS-first default is approved Claude and OpenAI models through Amazon Bedrock, with a coding client in front of them. The two typed-decision products at the end of this group are different in kind: they answer a typed question with a calibrated probability instead of generating text, so judge them on decision quality, not on chat ability. Jev 1.14 added a Box primitive for images; Strands Decider documents Choice, Score and Noul only, with no Box. [25][24]

Command-line clients in this group ship several times a week. Treat every version below as a dated snapshot, and confirm the current release before adoption.

AI gateways and routing

A gateway puts many model providers behind one endpoint, with routing, fallbacks, keys, budgets and guardrail hooks. Hosted routers are the fastest route; a self-hosted gateway fits a team that already runs the platform it sits on. Two entries here need care: the Portkey open-source gateway is dormant since the Palo Alto Networks acquisition, and the Envoy gateway has been renamed Agent Router. [27][29]

Context and memory

These products supply the information an agent works with: retrieval over enterprise documents, and memory of past sessions and preferences. The AWS-first route is the Managed Knowledge Base, generally available on 17 June 2026, with AgentCore Memory beside it. When you bring your own vector store, OpenSearch Serverless fits scale and hybrid search, and Aurora with pgvector fits data that already lives in PostgreSQL. Zep Community Edition is retired: it was deprecated on 2 April 2025, so do not adopt it. [17][21]

Harness and agent frameworks

The harness is the loop that calls the model, hands it tools, and decides when to continue or return a result. AgentCore Harness is the managed form of that loop: it is defined by configuration, powered by Strands, and generally available since June 2026. AgentCore Runtime is a different product, the hosting for agent code you write yourself. The frameworks below are the code-level alternative, for teams that want explicit control of the loop in Python or TypeScript. [18]

Microsoft Agent Framework reached 1.0 on 3 April 2026 and is the successor to AutoGen, which is archived. AG2 is a separate community fork of AutoGen, not Microsoft’s product. [34]

Agentic development environments

An agentic development environment supervises several tasks at once, each in its own workspace, with a person able to check and steer them. It is the Concepts answer to running work in parallel without losing track of what changed. Only one product in this radar is an environment in that sense. A coding client running several worktree sessions is not the same thing, and a worktree is not a security sandbox.

Verification

Verification checks whether work meets its requirements, and keeps that check independent of the agent that did the work. AgentCore Evaluations is the managed service for scoring agent behaviour, with 15 built-in evaluators. Bedrock Guardrails Automated Reasoning checks a response against formal-logic rules, but only in detect mode: it returns findings and your application decides what to do. CodeGuru Reviewer is in maintenance mode from 7 November 2025, with no new repository associations; that is not the same as end of support, which applies to CodeGuru Security. [14][15][16]

Sandbox and execution

A sandbox bounds the code an agent runs, but isolation is not the same as denying credentials, network or host access: those still need separate identity and egress controls. Nitro Sandboxes, launched on 9 November 2026, give each EKS pod, ECS task or EC2 workload its own hardware-isolated microVM. Nitro Enclaves are a different boundary: they protect sensitive data from the parent instance, and are not a code-execution sandbox. [12]

Lambda MicroVMs are a serverless form of the same idea, generally available from 22 June 2026. E2B is the hosted alternative, with an open-source runtime. [22][23]

Software factories

A software factory takes work from an issue to a pull request with as little hand assembly as possible: a cloud agent works on a branch and opens the change for review. This group is moving fast, and several entries are retiring. Google Jules has been read-only since 11 November 2026 and winds down on 31 December 2026. New installations of Amazon Q Developer for GitHub stop on 18 November 2026, with support ending on 30 January 2027. CodeCatalyst closed to new customers on 7 November 2025, and Aider has had no release since February 2026. [42][43][44][45]

AI workflow skill packs

Skill packs are reusable procedures for coding agents: a set of skill files that tell the agent how to plan, build, verify and review work. They differ in shape, so their counts are not comparable: Superpowers is a methodology that triggers itself, pstack is a Cursor-first set of playbooks entered by command, gstack organises the agent as a team of roles, and tstack covers the pull-request lifecycle. Pin a pack to a reviewed version or commit before adopting it, and check its licence: ub-mode has no licence at all, so it is not open source in the legal sense, and its final rule tells the agent to push to the main line. [52]
